Recurrent networks and LSTM, for programmers

The Elman recurrent cell and its shapes, unrolling in time and backpropagation through it (BPTT); the product of Jacobians that makes the gradient vanish or explode, measured on real networks, and norm clipping; the LSTM with its additive cell and three gates, the GRU, and the PyTorch conventions (order i, f, g, o and two bias vectors); RNN and LSTM cells from scratch in NumPy, forward and backward, verified against torch.nn.RNN and torch.nn.LSTM; and real training of an RNN, an LSTM and a GRU on a memory task with a truck's accelerometer, as the gap grows. With a worked example: three steps of a one-neuron LSTM, by hand.

Summary

  • A recurrent network applies the same cell at every step and passes its state to itself. Unrolled, it is a deep network with shared weights, and its backward gradient is a product of Jacobians : with PyTorch's initialization, the gradient that reaches the first of 66 readings is times the one at the last.
  • Memory task ("was there a harsh brake in the first 16 readings?", answered at the end): with a 2.5 s gap, 16-unit RNN, LSTM and GRU all get more than 99% right; with 5 s and more, the RNN stays between 48.7% and 62.8% (nine training runs) and the LSTM and GRU between 99.2% and 99.9% (1,000 test segments, three seeds per gap).
  • The LSTM cell is updated by adding: its direct backward path is only multiplied by the forget gate . Opening that gate at initialization (bias 3) matters: with PyTorch's bias of 0, two of three seeds do not learn with a 10 s gap.
  • Our NumPy RNN and LSTM cells match PyTorch in states and gradients up to , and central differences up to .
x₁ … x_T→ cell (RNN · LSTM · GRU)→ h_T→ linear → σ→ harsh?

§1 · The problem

Variable-length sequences, with distant dependencies

A trip is a sequence whose length changes from one trip to another, and where what matters at step may depend on something that happened long before. A dense network (topic 3) needs a fixed-size input. A 1D CNN (topic 8) accepts any length, but each output depends only on its receptive field: seeing 100 readings back takes many layers.

A recurrent network sums up the past in a fixed-size vector, the state , and updates it with each reading: . It is a dynamical system with state, like a Kalman filter (ML series), but with the update rule learned from data instead of derived from a physical model; and unlike a Markov chain (ML series), the state is continuous and does not have to be enumerated.

§2 · The Elman cell

A layer applied at every step, with the same weights

With input and state :

The parameters do not depend on : there are , plus the output. In PyTorch, nn.RNN stores weight_ih_l0 (), weight_hh_l0 () and two biases, bias_ih_l0 and bias_hh_l0, which always appear added together: . It is redundant (it comes from the cuDNN implementation) and makes PyTorch count : with and , 304 parameters plus 17 for the output, 321.

There are three ways to read the output. Many to one: only from (classifying a segment, the task in §6). Aligned many to many: at every step (labeling or forecasting, §7). Encoder-decoder: one network reads the whole input and another, starting from its final state, generates a sequence of a different length (Cho et al., 2014). Layers can be stacked (the output of one is the input of the next) and the sequence can be read in both directions (bidirectional) when the answer does not have to be given on the fly.

§3 · Backpropagation through time

The product of Jacobians: vanish or explode

Unrolled, the network is a graph of layers that share . The backpropagation from topic 5 on that graph is BPTT (Werbos, 1990): the gradient of each shared weight is the sum of its gradients at each step. With and (what arrives from the output at step plus what arrives from step ):

Chaining the chain rule (math topic 16) from the end back to step :

Since , if the largest singular value of is less than 1 the gradient decays at least exponentially with distance (Bengio, Simard and Frasconi, 1994; Pascanu, Mikolov and Bengio, 2013, give the condition). If it is greater than 1, it can grow exponentially. We measure it with a 16-unit RNN whose starts as , with orthogonal (all its singular values equal ), and on the networks of §6 before and after training:

bptt.py · ‖∂z/∂h_t‖ in the networks of §6 · actual output

"""The echo of the gradient: how much of the gradient of the final answer z (the logit) reaches each step t, ‖∂z/∂h_t‖,
for the 16-unit RNN and LSTM, before training (seed-0 initial weights) and once trained.
For the LSTM also ‖∂z/∂c_t‖, the gradient that travels along the conveyor belt. Mean over 200 test segments."""
import json, os
import numpy as np
import torch
from datos import HUECOS, L0, datos
from modelos import Lectora, ESCALA

os.chdir(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))


def eco(m, X):
    """Runs the network by hand with the same weights to keep the gradient of each h_t (and c_t)."""
    P = {k: v.detach() for k, v in m.state_dict().items()}
    W, U, b = P["rec.weight_ih_l0"], P["rec.weight_hh_l0"], P["rec.bias_ih_l0"] + P["rec.bias_hh_l0"]
    x = torch.tensor(X)[:, :, None] / ESCALA; n, T, _ = x.shape; H = U.shape[1]
    h, c, hs, cs = torch.zeros(n, H, requires_grad=True), torch.zeros(n, H), [], []
    for t in range(T):
        z = x[:, t] @ W.T + h @ U.T + b
        if m.tipo == "RNN":
            h = torch.tanh(z)
        else:
            i, f, g, o = torch.sigmoid(z[:, :H]), torch.sigmoid(z[:, H:2 * H]), torch.tanh(z[:, 2 * H:3 * H]), torch.sigmoid(z[:, 3 * H:])
            c = f * c + i * g; c.retain_grad(); cs.append(c)
            h = o * torch.tanh(c)
        h.retain_grad(); hs.append(h)
    logit = h @ P["out.weight"][0] + P["out.bias"][0]
    logit.sum().backward()
    gh = np.array([v.grad.norm(dim=1).mean().item() for v in hs])
    gc = np.array([v.grad.norm(dim=1).mean().item() for v in cs]) if cs else None
    return gh, gc


if __name__ == "__main__":
    R = {}
    print("‖∂z/∂h_t‖ k steps from the end, relative to k = 0 (mean over 200 test segments)")
    for G in HUECOS:
        _, _, (Xt, _, _) = datos(G)
        for tipo in ("RNN", "LSTM"):
            torch.manual_seed(0); ini = Lectora(tipo, 16)                       # the same weights it started training with
            fin = Lectora(tipo, 16); fin.load_state_dict(torch.load(f"red_{tipo}16_G{G}.pt"))
            for cuando, m in (("inicio", ini), ("entrenada", fin)):
                gh, gc = eco(m, Xt[:200])
                R[f"{tipo}|{cuando}|{G}"] = [float(f"{v:.4g}") for v in gh / gh[-1]]
                if gc is not None:
                    R[f"{tipo}|{cuando}|{G}|c"] = [float(f"{v:.4g}") for v in gc / gh[-1]]
                if G in (50, 100):
                    T = L0 + G; ks = [k for k in (0, 10, 25, 50, 75, 100, T - 1) if k < T]
                    nombre = {"inicio": "untrained", "entrenada": "trained"}[cuando]
                    print(f"gap {G:3d} {tipo:4s} {nombre:9s} " + "  ".join(f"k={k}: {gh[T - 1 - k] / gh[-1]:.1e}" for k in ks))
    json.dump(R, open("bptt.json", "w", encoding="utf-8"), separators=(",", ":"))
# ‖∂z/∂h_t‖ k steps from the end, relative to k = 0 (mean over 200 test segments)
# gap  50 RNN  untrained k=0: 1.0e+00  k=10: 1.7e-03  k=25: 2.3e-07  k=50: 9.0e-14  k=65: 1.1e-17
# gap  50 RNN  trained   k=0: 1.0e+00  k=10: 1.6e-01  k=25: 9.2e-03  k=50: 6.7e-05  k=65: 3.4e-06
# gap  50 LSTM untrained k=0: 1.0e+00  k=10: 2.5e-02  k=25: 1.8e-02  k=50: 1.5e-02  k=65: 2.0e-02
# gap  50 LSTM trained   k=0: 1.0e+00  k=10: 5.0e-03  k=25: 4.4e-03  k=50: 2.0e-02  k=65: 1.7e-01
# gap 100 RNN  untrained k=0: 1.0e+00  k=10: 1.7e-03  k=25: 2.3e-07  k=50: 8.9e-14  k=75: 3.3e-20  k=100: 1.3e-26  k=115: 1.7e-30
# gap 100 RNN  trained   k=0: 1.0e+00  k=10: 1.6e-01  k=25: 1.5e-02  k=50: 2.4e-04  k=75: 4.4e-06  k=100: 7.7e-08  k=115: 4.7e-09
# gap 100 LSTM untrained k=0: 1.0e+00  k=10: 1.7e-02  k=25: 6.5e-03  k=50: 1.6e-03  k=75: 6.3e-04  k=100: 3.8e-04  k=115: 4.6e-04
# gap 100 LSTM trained   k=0: 1.0e+00  k=10: 5.2e-03  k=25: 4.0e-03  k=50: 3.7e-03  k=75: 5.8e-03  k=100: 2.4e-02  k=115: 1.8e-01

With PyTorch's initialization (), the RNN's gradient is divided by between 1.8 and 1.9 at every step: after 65 steps, , below the precision with which it is added to the gradients of the recent readings. Once trained, the RNN learns to keep a bit more (), but it no longer helps: training got stuck at "say 50%". The LSTM starts with at the same distance, and once trained the gradient rises when it reaches the start: it has learned that the answer is there.

recorte.py · U = ρQ before training, and norm clipping · actual output

"""The exploding gradient and clipping. A 16-unit RNN whose recurrent matrix U starts as
ρ · (an orthogonal matrix): with ρ < 1 the echo dies out and with ρ > 1 it can grow step by step. Then the same
RNN with ρ = 1.5 trained with plain gradient descent (rate 0.05, batches of 32, 10 epochs, gap of 25
readings), without clipping and clipping the gradient norm to 1 (Pascanu, Mikolov and Bengio, 2013)."""
import numpy as np
import torch
from torch import nn
from datos import datos
from modelos import Lectora
from bptt import eco

torch.set_num_threads(4)
(X, Y, _), (Xv, Yv, _), (Xt, _, _) = datos(25)
Xtr, Ytr, Xva, Yva = (torch.tensor(a, dtype=torch.float64) for a in (X, Y, Xv, Yv))


def red(rho, seed=0):
    torch.manual_seed(seed); m = Lectora("RNN", 16)
    with torch.no_grad():
        q, _ = torch.linalg.qr(torch.randn(16, 16)); m.rec.weight_hh_l0.copy_(rho * q)
    return m


print("‖∂z/∂h_t‖ k steps from the end, relative to k = 0, before training (200 segments of 41 readings)")
for rho in (0.5, 0.9, 1.0, 1.5, 3.0):
    gh, _ = eco(red(rho), Xt[:200])
    print(f"ρ = {rho:3.1f}: " + "  ".join(f"k={k}: {gh[-1 - k] / gh[-1]:.1e}" for k in (1, 5, 10, 20, 40)))

perd = nn.functional.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits
print("ρ = 1.5, plain gradient descent · validation accuracy at the end of each epoch")
for recorte in (None, 1.0):
    m = red(1.5); opt = torch.optim.SGD(m.parameters(), lr=0.05); g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(1)
    normas, saltos, accs = [], [], []
    for ep in range(10):
        orden = torch.randperm(len(Ytr), generator=g)
        for k in range(0, len(Ytr), 32):
            j = orden[k:k + 32]; opt.zero_grad(); perd(m(Xtr[j]), Ytr[j]).backward()
            normas.append(nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(m.parameters(), recorte if recorte else float("inf")).item())
            antes = [p.detach().clone() for p in m.parameters()]; opt.step()
            saltos.append(float(sum(((p.detach() - a) ** 2).sum() for p, a in zip(m.parameters(), antes)) ** 0.5))
        with torch.no_grad():
            accs.append(((m(Xva) > 0).double() == Yva).double().mean().item())
    print(f"{'clipping at 1' if recorte else 'no clipping  '}: gradient norm median {np.median(normas):.2f}, max {max(normas):.1f};"
          f" largest weight step {max(saltos):.2f}; accuracy {' '.join(f'{a:.0%}' for a in accs)}")
# ‖∂z/∂h_t‖ k steps from the end, relative to k = 0, before training (200 segments of 41 readings)
# ρ = 0.5: k=1: 4.9e-01  k=5: 2.6e-02  k=10: 7.0e-04  k=20: 5.0e-07  k=40: 2.8e-13
# ρ = 0.9: k=1: 8.8e-01  k=5: 4.6e-01  k=10: 2.3e-01  k=20: 5.5e-02  k=40: 3.1e-03
# ρ = 1.0: k=1: 9.4e-01  k=5: 6.1e-01  k=10: 4.8e-01  k=20: 2.2e-01  k=40: 6.9e-02
# ρ = 1.5: k=1: 1.1e+00  k=5: 1.3e+00  k=10: 1.6e+00  k=20: 2.8e+00  k=40: 3.4e+01
# ρ = 3.0: k=1: 1.3e+00  k=5: 3.6e+00  k=10: 1.3e+01  k=20: 2.3e+02  k=40: 4.2e+04
# ρ = 1.5, plain gradient descent · validation accuracy at the end of each epoch
# no clipping  : gradient norm median 0.72, max 8.4; largest weight step 0.42; accuracy 52% 67% 51% 54% 51% 51% 49% 48% 46% 49%
# clipping at 1: gradient norm median 3.14, max 110.1; largest weight step 0.05; accuracy 72% 92% 97% 92% 98% 98% 94% 99% 95% 99%

With the gradient falls to in 40 steps; with it grows 34 times and with , 42,000 times (tanh saturation slows it down, but not enough). The explosion breaks gradient descent: without clipping, with weight steps of up to 0.42, the network reaches 67% in the second epoch, falls apart and ends at 49%. Clipping the norm of the full gradient to a maximum keeps the direction and limits the step:

With no step exceeds , even when the gradient reaches 110, and the same network reaches 99%. That is what torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_ does, and we use it in every training run in §6. With Adam the effect is smaller, because Adam already normalizes each step, but a huge gradient still contaminates its moving averages. Against vanishing, clipping does nothing: you need another architecture.

§4 · LSTM and GRU

An additive cell with gates

The LSTM (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997, with the forget gate of Gers, Schmidhuber and Cummins, 2000) adds a cell and three gates. In the order in which PyTorch stacks the blocks of weight_ih_l0 , weight_hh_l0 and the two biases :

is the input gate, the forget gate, the candidate (what would be written) and the output gate. Each gate is a vector in that multiplies element by element. The key is the sum in : the direct Jacobian of the cell is diagonal,

with no or tanh derivatives in between (there are more paths, through and the gates, but this one is enough for the gradient to survive). If the network learns in a unit, that unit is an accumulator: it keeps what it wrote and lets the gradient through intact. That is why it pays to start with the forget gate open: we initialize , (Jozefowicz, Zaremba and Sutskever, 2015, recommend 1; with gaps of 100 readings, 3 worked better in our tests).

Shapes and parameters. , or counting PyTorch's two biases: 1,216 with , four times the RNN. The order matters: Keras uses the same one (it calls it i, f, c, o), but not every implementation does; reading the blocks in the wrong order gives another network (check.py, below, tries it with i, f, o, g).

GRU (Cho et al., 2014): two gates and no separate cell, in PyTorch's order r, z, n:

Here the gate acts as both forget and input gate (what is kept and what is written add up to 1), and the state is updated additively like the LSTM cell. Careful: in PyTorch's GRU the two biases of are not redundant, because sits inside . It has parameters in PyTorch: 912 with . We also give an initial bias of 3, so it starts by keeping the state.

§5 · From scratch

RNN and LSTM cells in NumPy, forward and backward

On the forward pass we keep everything the backward pass needs: the states and and the four gates at each step. On the backward pass we run through the sequence in reverse carrying two gradients, and . In the LSTM, with already accumulated:

celdas.py · RNN and LSTM from scratch, with PyTorch's conventions

"""An RNN cell (tanh) and an LSTM cell from scratch in NumPy, forward and backward along the whole
sequence (backpropagation through time). Same conventions as PyTorch: X is (n, T, D), the input weights
are (rows, D), the recurrent ones (rows, H), and the LSTM stacks its four blocks in the order i, f, g, o."""
import numpy as np


def sigmoide(z):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- RNN: h_t = tanh(W x_t + U h_{t-1} + b)
def rnn_adelante(X, W, U, b, h0):
    n, T, _ = X.shape
    Hs = np.zeros((n, T + 1, U.shape[0])); Hs[:, 0] = h0           # Hs[:, t + 1] = h_t; Hs[:, 0] = h_0
    for t in range(T):
        Hs[:, t + 1] = np.tanh(X[:, t] @ W.T + Hs[:, t] @ U.T + b)
    return Hs[:, 1:], (X, W, U, Hs)


def rnn_atras(dH, cache):
    """dH: ∂L/∂h_t arriving from above at each step (n, T, H). Returns ∂L/∂X, ∂W, ∂U, ∂b, ∂h_0."""
    X, W, U, Hs = cache
    dX, dW, dU, db = np.zeros_like(X), np.zeros_like(W), np.zeros_like(U), np.zeros(U.shape[0])
    dh = np.zeros_like(Hs[:, 0])                                    # what arrives from the next step
    for t in reversed(range(X.shape[1])):
        dh = dh + dH[:, t]
        da = dh * (1 - Hs[:, t + 1] ** 2)                           # through tanh: tanh' = 1 − h²
        dW += da.T @ X[:, t]; dU += da.T @ Hs[:, t]; db += da.sum(0)
        dX[:, t] = da @ W
        dh = da @ U                                                 # towards h_{t-1}: the product that vanishes
    return dX, dW, dU, db, dh


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- LSTM
def lstm_adelante(X, W, U, b, h0, c0):
    """z = W x_t + U h_{t-1} + b, split into four blocks of H: i, f, o with sigmoid and g with tanh.
    c_t = f ⊙ c_{t-1} + i ⊙ g ;  h_t = o ⊙ tanh(c_t)."""
    n, T, _ = X.shape; H = U.shape[1]
    Hs = np.zeros((n, T + 1, H)); Cs = np.zeros((n, T + 1, H)); Hs[:, 0], Cs[:, 0] = h0, c0
    P = np.zeros((n, T, 4, H))                                      # gates i, f, g, o at each step
    for t in range(T):
        z = (X[:, t] @ W.T + Hs[:, t] @ U.T + b).reshape(n, 4, H)
        i, f, g, o = sigmoide(z[:, 0]), sigmoide(z[:, 1]), np.tanh(z[:, 2]), sigmoide(z[:, 3])
        Cs[:, t + 1] = f * Cs[:, t] + i * g
        Hs[:, t + 1] = o * np.tanh(Cs[:, t + 1])
        P[:, t] = np.stack([i, f, g, o], 1)
    return Hs[:, 1:], Cs[:, 1:], (X, W, U, Hs, Cs, P)


def lstm_atras(dH, cache, dC=None):
    """dH (and optionally dC): gradients arriving from above on h_t (and c_t). Returns ∂X, ∂W, ∂U, ∂b, ∂h_0, ∂c_0."""
    X, W, U, Hs, Cs, P = cache
    n, T, _ = X.shape; H = U.shape[1]
    dX, dW, dU, db = np.zeros_like(X), np.zeros_like(W), np.zeros_like(U), np.zeros(4 * H)
    dh, dc = np.zeros((n, H)), np.zeros((n, H))
    for t in reversed(range(T)):
        i, f, g, o = P[:, t, 0], P[:, t, 1], P[:, t, 2], P[:, t, 3]
        tc = np.tanh(Cs[:, t + 1])
        dh = dh + dH[:, t]
        dc = dc + dh * o * (1 - tc ** 2) + (0 if dC is None else dC[:, t])
        dz = np.concatenate([dc * g * i * (1 - i),                  # input gate
                             dc * Cs[:, t] * f * (1 - f),           # forget gate
                             dc * i * (1 - g ** 2),                 # candidate
                             dh * tc * o * (1 - o)], 1)             # output gate
        dW += dz.T @ X[:, t]; dU += dz.T @ Hs[:, t]; db += dz.sum(0)
        dX[:, t] = dz @ W
        dh = dz @ U
        dc = dc * f                                                 # the conveyor belt: only multiplied by f
    return dX, dW, dU, db, dh, dc

check.py · against torch.nn.RNN, torch.nn.LSTM and their autograd (PyTorch 2.15, CPU, float64)

"""celdas.py against torch.nn.RNN and torch.nn.LSTM (copying the weights) and their autograd, in float64, and against
central differences. Maximum absolute error of the states and of each gradient."""
import numpy as np
import torch
from torch import nn
from celdas import rnn_adelante, rnn_atras, lstm_adelante, lstm_atras

torch.set_default_dtype(torch.float64)
rng = np.random.default_rng(9)
torch.manual_seed(9)                                # the random weights of nn.RNN and nn.LSTM, reproducible
err = lambda a, t: float(np.max(np.abs(a - (t.detach().numpy() if torch.is_tensor(t) else t))))
print(f"PyTorch {torch.__version__}, float64 · maximum absolute error")
n, T, D, H = 4, 30, 3, 5
X, h0, c0 = rng.normal(size=(n, T, D)), rng.normal(size=(n, H)), rng.normal(size=(n, H))
dH = rng.normal(size=(n, T, H))                     # any gradient "from above" on each h_t

# ---------- RNN ----------
red = nn.RNN(D, H, batch_first=True)                 # PyTorch's random weights
W, U = red.weight_ih_l0.detach().numpy(), red.weight_hh_l0.detach().numpy()
b = (red.bias_ih_l0 + red.bias_hh_l0).detach().numpy()   # PyTorch has two biases; only their sum matters
Hn, cache = rnn_adelante(X, W, U, b, h0)
dX, dW, dU, db, dh0 = rnn_atras(dH, cache)
Xt, h0t = torch.tensor(X, requires_grad=True), torch.tensor(h0[None], requires_grad=True)
Ht, _ = red(Xt, h0t); (Ht * torch.tensor(dH)).sum().backward()
print(f"RNN  T={T}:  h {err(Hn, Ht):.1e}  ∂x {err(dX, Xt.grad):.1e}  ∂W {err(dW, red.weight_ih_l0.grad):.1e}"
      f"  ∂U {err(dU, red.weight_hh_l0.grad):.1e}  ∂b_ih {err(db, red.bias_ih_l0.grad):.1e}"
      f"  ∂b_hh {err(db, red.bias_hh_l0.grad):.1e}  ∂h0 {err(dh0, h0t.grad[0]):.1e}")

# ---------- LSTM ----------
red = nn.LSTM(D, H, batch_first=True)
W, U = red.weight_ih_l0.detach().numpy(), red.weight_hh_l0.detach().numpy()   # (4H, D) and (4H, H), blocks i, f, g, o
b = (red.bias_ih_l0 + red.bias_hh_l0).detach().numpy()
Hn, Cn, cache = lstm_adelante(X, W, U, b, h0, c0)
dX, dW, dU, db, dh0, dc0 = lstm_atras(dH, cache)
Xt = torch.tensor(X, requires_grad=True)
h0t, c0t = torch.tensor(h0[None], requires_grad=True), torch.tensor(c0[None], requires_grad=True)
Ht, (hT, cT) = red(Xt, (h0t, c0t)); (Ht * torch.tensor(dH)).sum().backward()
print(f"LSTM T={T}:  h {err(Hn, Ht):.1e}  c_T {err(Cn[:, -1], cT[0]):.1e}  ∂x {err(dX, Xt.grad):.1e}"
      f"  ∂W {err(dW, red.weight_ih_l0.grad):.1e}  ∂U {err(dU, red.weight_hh_l0.grad):.1e}"
      f"  ∂b {err(db, red.bias_ih_l0.grad):.1e}  ∂h0 {err(dh0, h0t.grad[0]):.1e}  ∂c0 {err(dc0, c0t.grad[0]):.1e}")

# the gate order matters: reading the blocks in the wrong order (i, f, o, g) gives another network
i, f, g, o = np.split(W, 4); j, k, l, m = np.split(U, 4); bi, bf, bg, bo = np.split(b, 4)
H2, _, _ = lstm_adelante(X, np.r_[i, f, o, g], np.r_[j, k, m, l], np.r_[bi, bf, bo, bg], h0, c0)
print(f"LSTM with the blocks read in the order i, f, o, g: h differs by {err(H2, Ht):.2f}")

# ---------- central differences on a scalar loss ----------
Wl, Ul, bl = rng.normal(size=(4 * H, D)) * 0.5, rng.normal(size=(4 * H, H)) * 0.5, rng.normal(size=4 * H) * 0.5
C = rng.normal(size=(n, T, H))
perdida = lambda U_: float((C * lstm_adelante(X, Wl, U_, bl, h0, c0)[0]).sum())
_, _, cache = lstm_adelante(X, Wl, Ul, bl, h0, c0); dUl = lstm_atras(C, cache)[2]
eps, num = 1e-6, np.zeros_like(Ul)
for idx in np.ndindex(Ul.shape):
    Up, Um = Ul.copy(), Ul.copy(); Up[idx] += eps; Um[idx] -= eps
    num[idx] = (perdida(Up) - perdida(Um)) / (2 * eps)
print(f"LSTM: ∂U against central differences (h = 1e-6): {np.max(np.abs(num - dUl)):.1e}")

# ---------- the trained LSTM (comparar.py), forward with celdas.py only ----------
from datos import datos
from modelos import Lectora, ESCALA
m = Lectora("LSTM", 16); m.load_state_dict(torch.load("red_LSTM16_G100.pt"))
P = {k: v.detach().numpy() for k, v in m.state_dict().items()}
_, _, (Xte, Yte, _) = datos(100)
Hn, _, _ = lstm_adelante(Xte[:, :, None] / ESCALA, P["rec.weight_ih_l0"], P["rec.weight_hh_l0"],
                         P["rec.bias_ih_l0"] + P["rec.bias_hh_l0"], np.zeros((len(Xte), 16)), np.zeros((len(Xte), 16)))
z = Hn[:, -1] @ P["out.weight"][0] + P["out.bias"][0]
with torch.no_grad():
    zt = m(torch.tensor(Xte)).numpy()
print(f"trained LSTM, 1,000 segments of 116 readings: logits against PyTorch {np.max(np.abs(z - zt)):.1e},"
      f" accuracy {np.mean((z > 0) == Yte):.1%}")

# RNN  T=30:  h 2.2e-16  ∂x 3.3e-16  ∂W 7.1e-15  ∂U 2.7e-15  ∂b_ih 5.3e-15  ∂b_hh 7.1e-15  ∂h0 4.4e-16
# LSTM T=30:  h 1.1e-16  c_T 1.1e-16  ∂x 1.7e-16  ∂W 1.3e-15  ∂U 2.2e-16  ∂b 1.8e-15  ∂h0 8.3e-17  ∂c0 1.0e-16

States and gradients match PyTorch within float64 rounding (the largest error, , in the RNN's and , which add up 30 steps). The gradients of bias_ih and bias_hh are the same , as they should be for two biases that only appear added together. Reading the blocks in the order i, f, o, g changes the states by up to 0.46. Central differences give , the expected error with . And the trained LSTM from §6 with a 100-reading gap, run with celdas.py only, gives the same logits as PyTorch on the 1,000 test segments.

§6 · Real comparison

RNN, LSTM and GRU against a longer and longer gap

The data are the accelerometer data from topic 8 (10 Hz, m/s², Gaussian noise with ). Each segment starts with 16 readings containing a braking, harsh (depth between 3.6 and 5.5 m/s²) or gentle (between 1 and 2.4), and continues with readings of normal driving: on average one event every 25 readings among gentle braking (up to 2.2 m/s²), pothole ( and with between 2.5 and 5) and speed-up, with no harsh brake at all. The label is the fleet rule on the clean signal of the start (mean of 5 readings below ). Half and half of each class. Applying the rule to the noisy start gets 99.6–99.9% right; applying it to the last 16 readings, 50%.

All three networks read the readings divided by 4 and answer with a linear layer on . They are trained the same way: Adam with rate 0.003, batches of 32, 60 epochs, binary cross-entropy (topic 4, topic 6), norm clipping at 1, and we keep the epoch with the best accuracy on 500 validation segments. 2,000 training segments per gap, float64, fixed seeds.

datos.py · the segments

"""Data for topic 9: segments of a truck's longitudinal accelerometer (10 readings per second, in m/s²;
below 0 the truck is braking), as in topic 8, but now of variable length and read step by step.

The memory question: "was there a harsh brake at the start?". Each segment starts with 16 readings (1.6 s) in which
the truck brakes, hard or gently, and continues with a gap of G readings of normal driving: vibration, gentle
braking, potholes and speed-ups, never another harsh brake. The network gives its answer at the end, once it has read everything.
The label is the fleet rule from topic 8 applied to the clean signal of the start: harsh if in some half
second (5 readings) the mean deceleration goes past 3 m/s²."""
import numpy as np

FS = 10                     # readings per second
L0 = 16                     # readings of the start, where the braking to remember is
UMBRAL = 3.0                # m/s² of mean deceleration over 0.5 s (the topic 8 rule)
RUIDO = 0.35                # m/s²: vibration measured by the accelerometer
HUECOS = (0, 10, 25, 50, 75, 100)   # readings between the start and the question


def media5(x):
    return np.convolve(x, np.ones(5) / 5, mode="valid")


def frenada(rng, prof, n_meseta):
    """Drops in 2–4 readings down to −prof, holds for n_meseta readings and comes back in 3–5 (as in topic 8)."""
    a, c = rng.integers(2, 5), rng.integers(3, 6)
    return np.r_[-prof * np.arange(1, a + 1) / a, -prof * np.ones(n_meseta), -prof * np.arange(c - 1, -1, -1) / c]


def distractores(rng, limpia, desde):
    """Normal driving in the gap: on average one event every 25 readings, gentle braking, pothole or speed-up."""
    n = len(limpia) - desde
    for _ in range(rng.poisson(n / 25)):
        tipo = rng.integers(3)
        if tipo == 0:                                       # gentle braking: never reaches harsh
            f = frenada(rng, rng.uniform(0.8, 2.2), rng.integers(2, 8))
            if len(f) <= n:
                s = desde + rng.integers(0, n - len(f) + 1); limpia[s:s + len(f)] += f
        elif tipo == 1 and n >= 2:                          # pothole: a 2-reading jolt, down and up
            b = desde + rng.integers(0, n - 1); A = rng.uniform(2.5, 5.0)
            limpia[b] -= A; limpia[b + 1] += A
        elif n >= 10:                                       # speed-up: positive, long and smooth
            m = rng.integers(10, min(21, n + 1)); b = desde + rng.integers(0, n - m + 1)
            limpia[b:b + m] += rng.uniform(0.8, 2.0) * np.sin(np.pi * np.arange(m) / (m - 1))


def tramo(rng, G, brusca):
    """One segment of 16 + G readings. Returns (noisy reading, clean signal, label)."""
    T = L0 + G
    t = np.arange(T)
    limpia = 0.25 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * (t / rng.uniform(40, 120) + rng.random())) + rng.normal(0, 0.1)
    while True:
        f = frenada(rng, rng.uniform(3.6, 5.5) if brusca else rng.uniform(1.0, 2.4), rng.integers(2, 6))
        if len(f) <= L0 - 1:
            break
    s = rng.integers(0, L0 - len(f) + 1)
    limpia[s:s + len(f)] += f
    base = limpia.copy()
    while True:                                             # the gap never has another harsh brake
        limpia = base.copy(); distractores(rng, limpia, L0)
        if G < 5 or media5(limpia[L0:]).min() >= -UMBRAL:
            break
    y = int(media5(limpia[:L0]).min() < -UMBRAL)
    return limpia + rng.normal(0, RUIDO, T), limpia, y


def conjunto(n, G, seed):
    """n segments with gap G, half with a harsh brake at the start. X: (n, 16 + G), y: (n,)."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    V = [tramo(rng, G, k % 2 == 0) for k in range(n)]
    orden = rng.permutation(n)
    X = np.array([V[k][0] for k in orden]); Y = np.array([V[k][2] for k in orden])
    LIM = np.array([V[k][1] for k in orden])
    return X, Y, LIM


def datos(G):
    """Training (2,000), validation (500) and test (1,000) for a gap G, with fixed seeds."""
    return conjunto(2000, G, 900 + G), conjunto(500, G, 1900 + G), conjunto(1000, G, 2900 + G)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for G in HUECOS:
        (X, Y, LIM), _, (Xt, Yt, _) = datos(G)
        regla = np.mean([(media5(x[:L0]).min() < -UMBRAL) == y for x, y in zip(Xt, Yt)])
        fin = np.mean([(media5(x[-L0:]).min() < -UMBRAL) == y for x, y in zip(Xt, Yt)]) if G >= L0 else float("nan")
        print(f"gap {G:3d}: {X.shape[1]:3d} readings, harsh {Y.mean():.1%} · rule on the noisy start {regla:.1%}"
              f" · same rule on the last 16 {fin:.1%} · lowest reading in the gap {LIM[:, L0:].min() if G else 0:.2f}")
# gap   0:  16 readings, harsh 49.8% · rule on the noisy start 99.7% · same rule on the last 16 nan% · lowest reading in the gap 0.00
# gap  10:  26 readings, harsh 49.7% · rule on the noisy start 99.7% · same rule on the last 16 nan% · lowest reading in the gap -6.20
# gap  25:  41 readings, harsh 49.9% · rule on the noisy start 99.7% · same rule on the last 16 50.0% · lowest reading in the gap -7.86
# gap  50:  66 readings, harsh 49.8% · rule on the noisy start 99.9% · same rule on the last 16 50.1% · lowest reading in the gap -9.53
# gap  75:  91 readings, harsh 49.6% · rule on the noisy start 99.6% · same rule on the last 16 50.1% · lowest reading in the gap -8.72
# gap 100: 116 readings, harsh 49.8% · rule on the noisy start 99.7% · same rule on the last 16 50.4% · lowest reading in the gap -9.83

modelos.py · the networks and the training loop

"""The networks of this topic, in PyTorch, and a training loop with fixed seeds (Adam, batches of 32, gradient
clipping). All three read the segment one reading at a time and answer with their last hidden state."""
import numpy as np
import torch
from torch import nn

torch.set_default_dtype(torch.float64)
ESCALA = 4.0                                   # m/s²: readings go in divided by 4, almost all of them in [−1, 1]
CAPAS = {"RNN": nn.RNN, "LSTM": nn.LSTM, "GRU": nn.GRU}


class Lectora(nn.Module):
    """recurrent cell (RNN with tanh, LSTM or GRU) with H units · linear H→1 on the last state."""
    def __init__(s, tipo="LSTM", H=16, sesgo_olvido=3.0):
        super().__init__()
        s.tipo, s.rec, s.out = tipo, CAPAS[tipo](1, H, batch_first=True), nn.Linear(H, 1)
        if tipo != "RNN" and sesgo_olvido is not None:
            # at the start, the gate that keeps the memory almost open: the LSTM forget gate (order i, f, g, o)
            # and the GRU update gate z (order r, z, n) take the second block of H rows
            with torch.no_grad():
                s.rec.bias_ih_l0[H:2 * H] = sesgo_olvido; s.rec.bias_hh_l0[H:2 * H] = 0.0

    def estados(s, x):                        # x: (n, T) in m/s² → hidden states h_1 … h_T: (n, T, H)
        return s.rec(x[:, :, None] / ESCALA)[0]

    def forward(s, x):
        return s.out(s.estados(x)[:, -1])[:, 0]           # logit of "there was a harsh brake at the start"


def n_param(m):
    return sum(p.numel() for p in m.parameters())


def entrenar(tipo, H, X, y, Xv, yv, epocas=60, lr=0.003, lote=32, recorte=1.0, seed=0, sesgo_olvido=3.0):
    """Adam with binary cross-entropy and clipping of the gradient norm. Keeps the epoch with the best
    validation accuracy. Returns the model and the curve (validation accuracy per epoch)."""
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    m = Lectora(tipo, H, sesgo_olvido)
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(m.parameters(), lr=lr)
    X, y, Xv, yv = (torch.tensor(a, dtype=torch.float64) for a in (X, y, Xv, yv))
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed + 1)
    perd = nn.functional.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits
    curva, mejor, estado = [], -1.0, None
    for _ in range(epocas):
        orden = torch.randperm(len(y), generator=g)
        for k in range(0, len(y), lote):
            j = orden[k:k + lote]
            opt.zero_grad(); perd(m(X[j]), y[j]).backward()
            if recorte:
                nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(m.parameters(), recorte)
            opt.step()
        with torch.no_grad():
            a = ((m(Xv) > 0).double() == yv).double().mean().item()
        curva.append(a)
        if a > mejor:
            mejor, estado = a, {k: v.clone() for k, v in m.state_dict().items()}
    m.load_state_dict(estado)
    return m, curva


def acierto(m, X, y):
    with torch.no_grad():
        return float(((m(torch.tensor(X)) > 0).numpy() == np.asarray(y)).mean())

comparar.py · actual output

"""Real training: RNN, LSTM and GRU with 16 units on the memory question, for each gap and three seeds
(in parallel, one process per network). The seed-0 networks and all the accuracies are saved in comparar.json.
Also the two minimal one-unit networks (gap of 25 readings) used by the toy and the worked example."""
import json, os, time
from multiprocessing import Pool
import torch
from datos import HUECOS, datos
from modelos import entrenar, acierto, n_param

os.chdir(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))


def una(args):
    tipo, H, G, seed, kw = args
    kw = dict(kw); extra = kw.pop("extra", "")
    torch.set_num_threads(1)
    (X, Y, _), (Xv, Yv, _), (Xt, Yt, _) = datos(G)
    m, curva = entrenar(tipo, H, X, Y, Xv, Yv, seed=seed, **kw)
    if seed == 0 and not extra:
        torch.save(m.state_dict(), f"red_{tipo}{H}_G{G}.pt")
    return dict(tipo=tipo, H=H, G=G, seed=seed, param=n_param(m), prueba=acierto(m, Xt, Yt), curva=curva, extra=extra)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    t0 = time.time()
    trabajos = [(t, 16, G, s, {}) for G in sorted(HUECOS, reverse=True) for t in ("LSTM", "GRU", "RNN") for s in (0, 1, 2)]
    trabajos += [(t, 1, 25, 0, dict(lr=0.01, sesgo_olvido=5.0)) for t in ("LSTM", "RNN")]
    # two controls: an RNN with as many parameters as the LSTM, and the LSTM with PyTorch's forget bias (0)
    trabajos += [("RNN", 32, 50, s, dict(extra="RNN with 32 units")) for s in (0, 1, 2)]
    trabajos += [("LSTM", 16, 100, s, dict(sesgo_olvido=None, extra="LSTM with forget bias 0")) for s in (0, 1, 2)]
    with Pool(15) as p:
        R = p.map(una, trabajos, chunksize=1)
    json.dump(R, open("comparar.json", "w", encoding="utf-8"))
    print(f"accuracy on 1,000 test segments (half with a harsh brake at the start) · {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")
    print("seed 0 (min–max over seeds 0, 1 and 2)")
    print(f"{'gap':18s}" + "".join(f"{t:24s}" for t in ("RNN", "LSTM", "GRU")))
    for G in HUECOS:
        fila = f"{G:3d} ({G / 10:4.1f} s)".ljust(18)
        for t in ("RNN", "LSTM", "GRU"):
            a = [r["prueba"] for r in R if r["tipo"] == t and r["H"] == 16 and r["G"] == G and not r["extra"]]
            fila += f"{a[0]:.1%} ({min(a):.1%}–{max(a):.1%})".ljust(24)
        print(fila)
    print("parameters:", {t: next(r["param"] for r in R if r["tipo"] == t and r["H"] == 16) for t in ("RNN", "LSTM", "GRU")})
    for e in ("RNN with 32 units", "LSTM with forget bias 0"):
        a = [r for r in R if r["extra"] == e]
        print(f"{e} ({a[0]['param']} parameters), gap {a[0]['G']}: " + ", ".join(f"{r['prueba']:.1%}" for r in a) + " (seeds 0, 1, 2)")
    for r in R:
        if r["H"] == 1:
            print(f"{r['tipo']} with a single unit ({r['param']} parameters), gap 25: {r['prueba']:.1%}")
# accuracy on 1,000 test segments (half with a harsh brake at the start) · 406 s
# seed 0 (min–max over seeds 0, 1 and 2)

#  10 ( 1.0 s)      99.5% (99.5%–99.7%)     99.5% (99.5%–99.7%)     99.5% (99.2%–99.6%)     
#  25 ( 2.5 s)      99.7% (50.9%–99.7%)     99.5% (99.0%–99.5%)     99.7% (99.6%–99.8%)     
#  50 ( 5.0 s)      50.1% (50.1%–53.2%)     99.6% (99.6%–99.9%)     99.8% (99.8%–99.9%)

# LSTM with forget bias 0 (1233 parameters), gap 100: 50.3%, 49.4%, 99.7% (seeds 0, 1, 2)
# LSTM with a single unit (18 parameters), gap 25: 99.8%
# RNN with a single unit (6 parameters), gap 25: 51.1%
RNN (321) LSTM (1,233) GRU (929)

Four takeaways. With short gaps there is no difference: up to 1 s, all three exceed 99%. At 2.5 s the RNN starts to fail: seed 0 learns (99.7%), another stays at 50.9%. At 5 s or more, the RNN does not learn (48.7–62.8% over nine training runs) and the LSTM and GRU do not drop below 99.2%. It is not a matter of size: a 32-unit RNN, with 1,153 parameters, almost as many as the LSTM, learns with a 5 s gap with only one seed out of three (98.6%; the others, 54.2% and 52.8%). And the LSTM is not magic either: with PyTorch's forget bias of 0, at a 10 s gap it learns with one seed out of three.

The simple version also uses an LSTM with a single unit (18 parameters, rate 0.01, forget bias 5): with a 2.5 s gap it gets 99.8% right, and the one-unit RNN, 51.1%. Its solution is interpretable: always, the cell grows positive without a harsh brake, and a harsh brake makes it negative; with , the recurrent weight of the input gate (2.74) closes it and the memory is locked. The worked example in §10 goes through it by hand. The data for the drawings are generated by toys.py:

#    forget gate learned: gets 998 of 1,000 right
#    forget gate fixed at 0.9: gets 556 of 1,000 right
# test trip 0: mean error RNN 2.73, LSTM 2.54, "stays the same" 3.69 km/h

§7 · Short memory

Predicting the speed: here the RNN is enough

Many to many: at each second , the network predicts the speed at from , with squared loss (, the input centered at 40 km/h and divided by 40). Synthetic 120 s trips with a target speed that changes, limited acceleration and noise. The useful information is in the last few seconds: speed, trend and whether it is approaching the target speed.

prever.py · actual output

"""Short memory: predict the truck's speed 3 seconds ahead from what it has read so far.
One output at every step (many to many). Here it is enough to remember the last few seconds: the RNN and the LSTM
are almost equally accurate, and both beat "stays the same" and "follows the trend"."""
import os
import numpy as np
import torch
from torch import nn

torch.set_default_dtype(torch.float64)
torch.set_num_threads(1)
os.chdir(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
T, AV = 120, 3                 # 120 s of speed, one reading per second; predicted 3 s ahead


def trayecto(rng):
    """Speed in km/h: the truck chases a target speed that changes (stop, street, avenue,
    highway) with limited acceleration and a little sensor noise."""
    v, obj, out = rng.uniform(0, 60), rng.choice([0, 30, 50, 80]), []
    for _ in range(T + AV):
        if rng.random() < 0.06:
            obj = rng.choice([0, 30, 50, 80])
        a = np.clip(0.35 * (obj - v), -6.0, 4.0)          # km/h per second: brakes harder than it accelerates
        v = max(0.0, v + a + rng.normal(0, 0.6))
        out.append(v)
    out = np.array(out)
    return out + rng.normal(0, 0.4, len(out))


def conjunto(n, seed):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    V = np.array([trayecto(rng) for _ in range(n)])
    return V[:, :T], V[:, AV:AV + T]                         # input v_1…v_120 and target v_4…v_123


class Prevision(nn.Module):
    def __init__(s, tipo, H=16):
        super().__init__()
        s.rec = {"RNN": nn.RNN, "LSTM": nn.LSTM}[tipo](1, H, batch_first=True); s.out = nn.Linear(H, 1)

    def forward(s, v):                                     # (n, T) km/h → (n, T) predicted km/h
        return 40 + 40 * s.out(s.rec((v[:, :, None] - 40) / 40)[0])[:, :, 0]


def entrenar(tipo, X, Y, epocas=30, seed=0):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    m = Prevision(tipo); opt = torch.optim.Adam(m.parameters(), lr=0.005)
    X, Y = torch.tensor(X), torch.tensor(Y); g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed + 1)
    for _ in range(epocas):
        orden = torch.randperm(len(X), generator=g)
        for k in range(0, len(X), 32):
            j = orden[k:k + 32]; opt.zero_grad()
            nn.functional.mse_loss(m(X[j]), Y[j]).backward()
            nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(m.parameters(), 1.0); opt.step()
    return m


X_TR, Y_TR = conjunto(1000, 91)
X_TE, Y_TE = conjunto(300, 92)
if __name__ == "__main__":
    ini = 10                                               # evaluated from second 10 on
    err = lambda P: float(np.mean(np.abs(P[:, ini:] - Y_TE[:, ini:])))
    print(f"mean error (km/h) predicting the speed {AV} s ahead, 300 test trips:")
    print(f"  \"stays the same\" (the last reading):   {err(X_TE):.2f}")
    tend = X_TE + AV * np.c_[np.zeros(len(X_TE)), np.diff(X_TE, axis=1)]
    print(f"  \"follows the trend\" (last change × 3): {err(tend):.2f}")
    P = {}
    for tipo in ("RNN", "LSTM"):
        m = entrenar(tipo, X_TR, Y_TR)
        with torch.no_grad():
            P[tipo] = m(torch.tensor(X_TE)).numpy()
        print(f"  {tipo:4s} with 16 units:                    {err(P[tipo]):.2f}")
        torch.save(m.state_dict(), f"prever_{tipo}.pt")
# mean error (km/h) predicting the speed 3 s ahead, 300 test trips:
#   "stays the same" (the last reading):   4.42
#   "follows the trend" (last change × 3): 3.93
#   RNN  with 16 units:                    3.19
#   LSTM with 16 units:                    3.08

Both networks cut the error by 28–30% compared with "stays the same" and by 19–22% compared with extrapolating the last change, and the difference between them (3.19 versus 3.08 km/h) is small. When the dependency is short, a plain RNN, with a quarter of the parameters, is a reasonable choice. The same goes for a 1D CNN with a receptive field of a few seconds, which also trains in parallel.

§8 · In practice

What is worth knowing when you use them

  • Sequences of different lengths in a batch. They are padded with zeros up to the longest one and PyTorch is given the length of each (nn.utils.rnn.pack_padded_sequence), so that the final state is the one of the last real reading and not of the padding.
  • Truncated BPTT. In very long sequences (a day of telemetry) you backpropagate only through blocks of steps, passing the state from one block to the next without a gradient (h.detach()). The cost is fixed per block, but the network cannot learn dependencies longer than except by chance.
  • Slow by construction. Step needs : it cannot be computed in parallel along time, and with long sequences training is slow even if the network is small.
  • Attention and Transformers. Instead of compressing the past into a vector, a Transformer looks at all positions at once and decides which ones to attend to. It parallelizes over time and does not have the vanishing-gradient problem along the sequence; in exchange, its cost grows with the square of the length. That is topic 11.
  • Inputs that are not numbers. CAN bus event types, fault codes or words are first turned into vectors with an embedding layer (topic 10).

§9 · Checklist

Before using a recurrent network

  • How far away is the information that matters? If it is a few steps, an RNN or a 1D CNN is enough; if it is tens or hundreds, use an LSTM or a GRU (or attention).
  • Scale the inputs so they stay close to [−1, 1]; the gates are sigmoids and saturate.
  • Clip the gradient norm (clip_grad_norm_, for example at 1) and watch its value during training.
  • Initialize the forget gate open (positive bias in the second block of the LSTM, in PyTorch's order i, f, g, o).
  • If you copy weights between libraries, check the gate order and add up PyTorch's two biases.
  • With sequences of different lengths, pack the batch so the padding is not read.
  • Train with several seeds: in memory tasks, learning or getting stuck depends on the starting point.
  • Verify your own implementations against torch.nn.RNN/LSTM and finite differences, including and .

§10 · Worked example

A one-neuron LSTM keeps a braking, by hand

The one-unit LSTM from §6, with its weights rounded to 2 decimals (that way it gets 998 of the 1,000 test segments right, the same as without rounding), on the first test segment with a harsh brake.

The situation. A truck leaves the loading dock and brakes hard. Its first readings are −2.25, −4.77, −4.96, −4.51, −5.07, −4.64, −3.55, −1.45 and 0.57 m/s², and the segment goes on up to 41 readings (4.1 s). The network has a single neuron with its cell. What does the braking write into the cell, why does the rest of the segment not erase it, and what does it answer at the end?

Example map

We go through steps 1, 2 and 3 of the segment, computing each gate with the learned weights; we jump to step 9, when the truck is no longer braking, to see why the memory is not erased; and we finish with the answer at step 41. All numbers are rounded to 4 decimals; the arithmetic uses all of them.

  1. The constants: where each number comes from.
  2. Step 1: almost nothing happens.
  3. Step 2: the braking is written into the cell.
  4. Step 3: the cell keeps going down.
  5. Step 9: the input gate has closed.
  6. Step 41: the answer, and what would happen without the belt.

  1. The constants: where each number comes from

    In words

    A one-unit LSTM has, for each of its four parts (input gate , forget gate , candidate and output gate ), a weight for the reading, a weight for what it showed at the previous step and a bias. That is 12 numbers, plus 2 for the output: 14 that do something. PyTorch stores 18, because it has two biases per part that only count as a sum.

    The math

    symbolvalue
    (i, f · g, o)    		what it is
    m/s²accelerometer reading (10 per second); negative = the truck is braking
    4m/s²the input scale: the network reads , so that almost all readings fall between −1 and 1, where the sigmoid and the tangent do not saturate
    −3.72 · −1.02
    1.87 · 5.49    		weights of the reading in each part, learned from 2,000 segments (§6); no units
    2.74 · −1.59
    −0.14 · 0.07    		weights of , what the neuron showed at the previous step
    −2.82 · 8.53
    1.06 · 4.11    		biases: each one is the sum of PyTorch's two, . The forget bias started at 5 and ended at 8.53
    −5.09 · 0.05the output: and probability of "harsh"
    (0, 1) · (−1, 1)sigmoid and hyperbolic tangent
    0 · 0at the start of the segment, the neuron has not read anything

    What it means: the forget bias, 8.53, is huge: even if the other terms subtract 1 or 2, stays above 0.999. The network has learned not to forget.

  2. Step 1: almost nothing happens

    In words

    The first reading is −2.25: the truck starts to brake. The network reads . Since , the terms with are zero.

    The math

    Why is g almost 0?

    The candidate is what the network would write. Its weight (1.87) times the reading (−0.5625) gives −1.05, and the bias, 1.06, cancels it almost exactly: a braking of 2.25 m/s² is the border between writing positive (not braking) and negative (braking hard).

    What it means: the cell barely moves (0.0026). A gentle braking leaves no trace.

  3. Step 2: the braking is written into the cell

    In words

    The reading drops to −4.77: now it really brakes hard. The network reads , and barely contributes.

    The math

    Where does each term come from?

    In , and . The weight of the reading in the input gate is negative: the harder the truck brakes, the wider it opens. In , beats the bias and what gets written is negative.

    What it means: the input gate opens to 83.5% and writes −0.82: the cell goes to −0.69. The almost closed output gate (0.08) hides the change from the outside: only drops to −0.05.

  4. Step 3: the cell keeps going down

    In words

    Another hard reading, −4.96 (the network reads −1.24). Now already counts a little.

    The math

    Why add instead of replace?

    The cell keeps what it had () and adds the new part (). Each step of hard braking subtracts about 0.7. In an RNN, the state would be rewritten completely, passing through a tangent.

    What it means: at step 8, when the braking ends, the cell has reached −3.61. That number is the memory.

  5. Step 9: the input gate has closed

    In words

    The truck is no longer braking: the reading is +0.57 (the network reads 0.1425). But now : as the cell went down, the output gate kept opening and became very negative. We come from .

    The math

    Who closes the gate?

    The term . Since the recurrent weight of the input gate is positive and is negative, the gate closes on its own (0.0031). Now what would be written is positive (0.90), but only 0.3% of it gets in.

    What it means: the neuron has turned into a locked switch. Neither the positive readings nor the potholes in the gap can bring the cell back to positive: over 32 more steps, it only rises from −3.61 to −3.43.

  6. Step 41: the answer, and what would happen without the belt

    In words

    At the end of the segment, . The output multiplies it by −5.09 and adds 0.05.

    The math

    And if the forget gate were 0.9?

    Over the 32 steps from 9 to 41, what was stored would be multiplied by : from −3.61 only −0.12 would be left, and what gets written in the gap would win. Running the whole segment with fixed, the cell ends at +0.75 and the answer is 0.042: it would say "there was no harsh brake". On the 1,000 test segments, with it gets 556 right; with the learned one, 998.

    What it means: 99.4% for "there was a harsh brake at the start", and the fleet says yes: correct. The memory crossed 32 readings because the cell is updated by adding and the forget gate is 0.9999: that is exactly the path along which, during training, the gradient traveled back to the braking.

ejemplo.py · reproduces the numbers above

"""The worked example: the one-unit LSTM (gap of 25 readings) with its weights rounded to 2 decimals,
step by step on the first test segment with a harsh brake. Prints each gate with 4 decimals."""
import math
import numpy as np
from datos import datos

W = [-3.72, -1.02, 1.87, 5.49]          # input weights, blocks i, f, g, o (PyTorch order)
U = [2.74, -1.59, -0.14, 0.07]          # weights of the previous state h_{t-1}
b = [-2.82, 8.53, 1.06, 4.11]           # b_ih + b_hh: PyTorch keeps two biases and only their sum matters
wo, bo = -5.09, 0.05                    # the output: z = wo·h_T + bo, probability σ(z)
sg = lambda z: 1 / (1 + math.exp(-z))

_, _, (X, Y, _) = datos(25)
x = [round(float(v), 2) for v in X[int(np.argmax(Y == 1))]]
print("readings 1 to 9:", x[:9], "· readings in total:", len(x))
h = c = 0.0
for t, v in enumerate(x, 1):
    xs = v / 4                                          # the reading goes in divided by 4
    zi, zf = W[0] * xs + U[0] * h + b[0], W[1] * xs + U[1] * h + b[1]
    zg, zo = W[2] * xs + U[2] * h + b[2], W[3] * xs + U[3] * h + b[3]
    i, f, g, o = sg(zi), sg(zf), math.tanh(zg), sg(zo)
    c_ant, c = c, f * c + i * g
    h_ant, h = h, o * math.tanh(c)
    if t in (1, 2, 3, 9, len(x)):
        print(f"step {t:2d}: x = {v:5.2f} (x/4 = {xs:.4f}), h_prev = {h_ant:.4f}, c_prev = {c_ant:.4f}")
        print("   terms W·x/4 and U·h_prev:", "  ".join(f"{n}: {W[k] * xs:.4f} {U[k] * h_ant:+.4f}" for k, n in enumerate("ifgo")))
        print(f"   z_i = {zi:.4f} → i = {i:.4f} · z_f = {zf:.4f} → f = {f:.5f} · z_g = {zg:.4f} → g = {g:.4f} · z_o = {zo:.4f} → o = {o:.4f}")
        print(f"   c = {f:.5f}·({c_ant:.4f}) + {i:.4f}·({g:.4f}) = {c:.4f} ;  h = {o:.4f}·tanh({c:.4f}) = {h:.4f}")
z = wo * h + bo
print(f"answer at the end: z = {wo}·({h:.4f}) + {bo} = {z:.4f} → probability of a harsh brake at the start {sg(z):.4f}")
print(f"if the forget gate were 0.9 for the 32 steps after reading 9: 0.9^32 = {0.9 ** 32:.4f}")

What would change in a real system

  • More signals: acceleration on all three axes, gyroscope, speed and position come in as or more channels.
  • More units and layers: 64–256 units, two stacked layers and dropout between them.
  • Whole trips: thousands of readings per trip, with truncated BPTT and the state passed between blocks.
  • Continuous answer: instead of one question at the end, one output per step that the fleet dashboard reads in real time.
